summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for RS-232-like serial hardware devices, the common serial port interface. It was replaced by RFC 1659.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of readings you can ask for from serial ports, the old round plugs on the back of computers, like whether a line is connected.

questions: how do you monitor serial ports with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management objects for serial ports and their control signals.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to monitor and manage RS-232 serial ports on computers connected to a network, including their speed, type, and control signal status.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1317 defines SNMP managed objects that expose details about RS-232-like ports (asynchronous and synchronous), their configuration parameters, and the status of incoming and outgoing control signals.
tldr.outcome: This MIB allows remote management of serial port hardware through standard SNMP tools, though it was later superseded by RFC 1659 with improvements.

today: RFC 1317 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1659, an improved version of the RS-232 MIB.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1317 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) in TCP/IP networks. Specifically, it defines managed objects for RS-232-like hardware devices: serial ports that are common on computers and network equipment.

The RFC applies to any system that has RS-232, RS-422, RS-423, V.35 or other asynchronous or synchronous serial ports that need to be managed remotely. A typical example is a port with modem signals, which is why this is useful for systems with terminal servers or network access servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Serial ports are old plugs on the back of computers. This document lets you check on them using a network tool called SNMP, the same tool that checks on routers and switches.

sections.title: The MIB Structure
sections.content:
The RS-232-like MIB is part of a family of related MIBs designed to work together. It sits at the physical layer, providing service to higher-level MIBs such as the Character MIB (for terminal connections) or the PPP MIB (for network connections). The design principle is that the RS-232 MIB represents the lowest hardware level, regardless of what application or protocol layer uses it.

The MIB comprises one base object and four main tables: a general port table with information common to all ports, an asynchronous port table for async-specific parameters, a synchronous port table for sync-specific parameters, and separate input and output signal tables. These tables are required only when applicable; for example, a system with only asynchronous ports does not include the synchronous port table.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the port as a post office mailbox. This document describes different types of mailboxes (fast or slow, one-way or two-way) and what you can check about each one.

sections.title: Port Types and Parameters
sections.content:
The general port table (rs232PortTable) contains entries for every RS-232-like port on the system. Each port entry includes a unique index, the hardware type (RS-232, RS-422, RS-423, or V.35), the number of input and output signals the software can detect, and the input and output speeds in bits per second.

For asynchronous ports, the MIB tracks additional parameters: the number of bits per character (5 to 8), the number of stop bits, the parity setting (none, odd, even, mark, or space), and an autobaud feature that can automatically detect input speed. It also provides error counters for parity errors, framing errors, and overrun errors on received data.

For synchronous ports, the MIB tracks the clock source (internal, external, or split between transmit and receive), and counters for frame check errors, transmit underrun errors, receive overrun errors, interrupted frames, and aborted frames.
sections.plainLanguage: Every port has a name and a speed setting. For old-fashioned sequential ports, we also track error counts to see if the connection is working well. For very fast ports, we track different kinds of errors.

sections.title: Signal Tables and Monitoring
sections.content:
The input signal table (rs232InSigTable) and output signal table (rs232OutSigTable) track the state of hardware control signals. These signals are named RTS (Request to Send), CTS (Clear to Send), DSR (Data Set Ready), DTR (Data Terminal Ready), RI (Ring Indicator), DCD (Received Line Signal Detector), SQ (Signal Quality Detector), SRS (Data Signaling Rate Selector), and their secondary variants.

For each signal, the tables record the current state (none, on, or off) and a counter of how many times the signal has changed from on to off or vice versa. This allows network administrators to verify that the expected handshaking signals are present and to detect when signals are toggling unexpectedly, which might indicate a hardware or connection problem.

The MIB is mandatory for all systems that have RS-232-like hardware ports supporting services managed through other MIBs. Implementations that do not have such ports are exempt from the requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: On a serial port, pins send little signals back and forth to say 'I'm ready to send' or 'I received your data.' We can check if those signals are on or off, and count how many times they change.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 1317 was published as a Proposed Standard in April 1992. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1659, which provides an improved version of the RS-232 MIB based on implementation experience.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is old; a better version exists now in RFC 1659 that fixes some problems.
